narrative: The model flagged you as a leaving risk, estimating a 46% chance that you will leave your job. That is not a certainty, but under the promotion process it is treated as a meaningful retention risk, which is why the promotion was denied. Of all the factors the model weighed, the most influential was that you reported no other job opportunities. This is common among employees predicted to stay—about 77% of them also had none—so it strongly pushed your prediction toward staying. The second most important factor was your 6–10 years in your current organization; roughly 35% of stayers share that tenure, and it also weighed toward staying. The third most important factor was your total 6–10 years of experience across all jobs, which pushed in the opposite direction, toward leaving. So the model’s result reflects a balance: two of the strongest signals are stabilizing, while your overall experience level adds leaving risk. Because the final risk was still high enough to cross the promotion threshold, the decision went against promotion. Next, you and your manager should discuss what would reduce that risk: clearer promotion criteria, recognition, development or training plans, workload and stress support, and whether pay, benefits, or work-life balance need attention. The organization should also confirm that a 46% estimated risk is being used fairly and that no protected characteristics influenced the decision.
